title: Converting Polar and Rectangular
short: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, and back again.
trouble: Students take θ = tan⁻¹(y/x) for a point in the second or third quadrant without adjusting.

blocks.html: A point described in polar coordinates also has rectangular coordinates. Converting between them is the same calculation as finding vector components and magnitudes.

Polar to rectangular: $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$. Rectangular to polar: $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$ and $\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$, with $\theta$ chosen in the quadrant where $(x, y)$ actually is. For equations, substitute $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$.

The point at distance $r$ along the ray at angle $\theta$ is the unit-circle point $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ stretched by $r$. Going back, $r$ is the distance from the origin (the Pythagorean theorem), and $\frac{y}{x}$ is the slope of the ray, which is $\tan\theta$.

blocks.name: polar
blocks.cap: The dashed lines show $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$.

blocks.title: Rectangular to polar
blocks.q: Convert $\left(-1, -\sqrt{3}\right)$ to polar coordinates with $r > 0$ and $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$.
steps: The point is in Quadrant III, so $\theta = \pi + \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3}$.

blocks.title: An equation
steps: Complete the square: $(x - 2)^2 + y^2 = 4$, a circle of radius $2$ centered at $(2, 0)$.

blocks.title: The other way
blocks.q: Write the line $x = 3$ as a polar equation solved for $r$.

blocks.html: Using $\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x}$ for a point in Quadrant II or III. For $\left(-1, -\sqrt{3}\right)$, $\tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} = \frac{\pi}{3}$ points into Quadrant I, the wrong side of the origin. Add $\pi$ when $x < 0$. Always check that your $(r, \theta)$ converts back to the original point.
